messages.author: f53f4ca2c430170d
messages.subject: output format
parts:
The csv_reader discussion started an output format discussion. If you have options that should be considered, or want to add to the discussion notes so far, they are here:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Output-format

I'm ok with doing exploration around suggested libraries but (as you'll see from the JSONlines entry) if I can't think of positives for an option, I won't try very hard. I think we can have this discussion now and settle on a overall strategy soon. I'm on board for implementing something (reasonable in scope) and, as suggested by Daniel, I'm hoping Bob can keep the design to something practical.

It would be great to make this a short-term project so if you have opinions pile on now... (here or at the Wiki page if it's more concrete). Having a good set format and tools to make it compatible with multiple interfaces would make the whole Stan-for-everything strategy a lot easier on interface maintainers.

Krzysztof

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] output format
parts:
We should be able to get away with two data formats (key/value pairs and vectors of samples)
which means only two output formats (sequences of key/value pairs and CSV files.
Altogether we could have as many output files as

config: key/value pairs
warmup_samples: csv
warmup_diagnostics: csv
samples: csv
diagnostics: csv

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] output format
parts:
JSON wold be reasonable for key-value pairs. It's
hard to write good C++ type-safe parsers that produce
objects from JSON as opposed to those that produce
parsers that accept callbacks. See the JSON parser
in stan/io.

When people say CSV here, are we really talking about
something with the flexibility of an R data frame? That
is, bunch of columns, each with a data type, then a bunch
of rows? Are the types just going to be integer, real, bool,
and string?

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] output format
parts:
> On Mar 17, 2016, at 4:19 PM, Krzysztof Sakrejda <krzysztof...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> On Thursday, March 17, 2016 at 3:35:49 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>> JSON wold be reasonable for key-value pairs. It's
>> hard to write good C++ type-safe parsers that produce
>> objects from JSON as opposed to those that produce
>> parsers that accept callbacks. See the JSON parser
>> in stan/io.
>
> We use callbacks everywhere else so they should be fine here too,
> but I looked at the JSON parser and did not find any examples of
> what the callback "Handler" is supposed to be. Is there an example
> somewhere?

Depends on what you want to do with it. Are you familiar
with SAX parsing of XML? It's the same pattern. There should
be some simple unit tests, but not a real application. The handler
would do thing like look along certain paths for numbers and
sum them. Or stuff them in a database or whatever.

>> When people say CSV here, are we really talking about
>> something with the flexibility of an R data frame? That
>> is, bunch of columns, each with a data type, then a bunch
>> of rows? Are the types just going to be integer, real, bool,
>> and string?
>
> I was assuming integer/double but without much type enforcement,
> sort of the way we currently write some sampler parameters (e.g.,
> tree_depth) as doubles even though they are really integers.

We don't do that in the C++. We promote ints to doubles, but *not*
vice-versa. It's a disaster for both speed and error handling.

R just works the way R works, and it seemed to much of people
to ask them to explicitly make 1 an integer because R just
straight-up assumes it's a double if not otherwise informed.
Our own data parsing does the opposite.

- Bob

> I don’t think we need chain ID in the CSV itself — right now
> having separate chains in separate files works perfectly
> well.

It works well unless you want to merge .csv files which currently means:

1) strip comments, including post-header comments
2) track chain id outside the file, maybe in the filename or somewhere else,
3) write it into each .csv file before/during a merge, potentially with an
iteration number.

This gets in the way of my workflow and I don't think it's an
unusual thing to want to concatenate matching .csv files. If there's
an actual downside to including a chain id (integer) could you
clarify what you're thinking of?

> with SAX parsing of XML? It's the same pattern. There should
> be some simple unit tests, but not a real application. The handler

Just looked up SAX parsing and found the abstract base class so it makes sense!

> >> When people say CSV here, are we really talking about
> >> something with the flexibility of an R data frame? That
> >> is, bunch of columns, each with a data type, then a bunch
> >> of rows? Are the types just going to be integer, real, bool,

> to ask them to explicitly make 1 an integer because R just
> straight-up assumes it's a double if not otherwise informed.
> Our own data parsing does the opposite.

Yeah... R... I'll leave that right there...

So far from the discussion with you and Michael it seems like multiple .csv files with
JSON for the key/value files should be a good overall text format. I'll summarise this
for the Wiki and see what else pops up.

Krzysztof

>
>>>> When people say CSV here, are we really talking about

>>

>> vice-versa. It's a disaster for both speed and error handling.
>
> right, we write integers and doubles as doubles. Reading is left to the
> interfaces but I'm not sure that we can really say "we don't do that"

> for a column called "n_leapfrog", they have to convert text to int. We
> don't have a binary format so I don't think you can blame that on the

I blame the interfaces. For the command line, the interface is the
command line itself, which is a string. So we pretty much have to
deal with converting strings. If we did this all in C++, all the types
would stay coherent. For R, if you write 1, R's the one that decided
that should be the same as writing c(1.0); you can coerce it to do something
else, but it's no longer idiomatic R (and it still trips people up because
we insist arrays are arrays, but if you pass in just c(1.0), it won't be
the right type because of the double-duty for scalars and 1D arrays.

>> R just works the way R works, and it seemed to much of people
>> to ask them to explicitly make 1 an integer because R just
>> straight-up assumes it's a double if not otherwise informed.
>> Our own data parsing does the opposite.
>

>
> So far from the discussion with you and Michael it seems like multiple .csv files with
> JSON for the key/value files should be a good overall text format. I'll summarise this
> for the Wiki and see what else pops up.

We can try to accomodate other interfaces other than CmdStan
with a format that includes the chain ID. I don't think it's
that much overhead to save, but it would mean a more complicated
CSV reader.

- Bob
